title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXX
paragraphs: An ill-timed attempt to give someone rest only tires them.—PASCAL.

Mr. Casaubon suffered no further attack as serious as the first. Within a few days he began returning to his ordinary state of health. Lydgate nevertheless seemed to consider the case worth close attention. Besides using his stethoscope, which was not yet a routine instrument in medical practice, he sat quietly beside his patient and observed him. When Mr. Casaubon asked about his condition, Lydgate attributed it to a common fault among intellectual men: working too intensely and with too little variation. The remedy was to accept a moderate amount of work and find different forms of recreation. On one visit Mr. Brooke, who was sitting with them, suggested fishing, as Cadwallader did, or setting up a room with a lathe and making toys, table legs, and similar things.

“In other words, you advise me to bring on my second childhood early,” poor Mr. Casaubon replied with some bitterness. Turning to Lydgate, he added, “I should find these activities about as restful as prisoners find picking apart old rope in a correctional institution.”

“I admit that amusement is a rather inadequate prescription,” said Lydgate, smiling. “It’s rather like telling someone to cheer up. Perhaps I should say you must accept a little boredom instead of continuing to work.”

“Exactly, exactly,” Mr. Brooke said. “Have Dorothea play backgammon with you in the evening. And during the day—shuttlecock! I can’t think of a better game. It used to be all the fashion. Of course, your eyes might not be up to that, Casaubon. Still, you have to relax. You could take up some light branch of study. Shells, for example—I always imagine the study of shells must be light. Or let Dorothea read you something entertaining. Smollett—‘Roderick Random,’ ‘Humphry Clinker.’ A little coarse in places, but now she’s married she can read anything. I remember laughing enormously. There’s a very funny passage about a postilion’s breeches. Nobody writes humor like that now. I’ve been through all these things myself, but they might be fresh to you.”

“As fresh as a diet of thistles” would have expressed Mr. Casaubon’s feelings. Out of respect for his wife’s uncle, however, he merely bowed in resignation and remarked that those books had doubtless “provided occupation for a certain class of intellect.”

“You see, Casaubon has been rather narrow,” the able magistrate told Lydgate once they were outside. “When you stop him doing his particular work, he doesn’t know where to turn. Very deep work, I believe—research and all that. I never let myself fall into that. I’ve always been versatile. A clergyman’s a little hemmed in, though. Now, if they made him a bishop! He wrote a very good pamphlet for Peel. There’d be more activity, more ceremony; he might put on some flesh. But I advise you to talk to Mrs. Casaubon. My niece is clever enough for anything. Tell her he needs liveliness and distraction. Set her thinking of ways to amuse him.”

Lydgate had already decided to speak to Dorothea. She had not been there for her uncle’s cheerful proposals for brightening life at Lowick, but she was usually beside her husband. The unmistakable anxiety in her face and voice whenever his health or feelings were involved made a drama Lydgate was inclined to observe. He told himself it was simply right to explain her husband’s likely future, but he also knew that a confidential conversation with her would interest him. Doctors like studying the mind, and such studies can tempt them into grave predictions that life and death easily overturn. Lydgate had often mocked this habit of needless prophecy. He intended to be cautious now.

He asked for Mrs. Casaubon and learned that she was out walking. As he was leaving, she and Celia appeared, their faces bright from battling the March wind. When he requested a private word, Dorothea opened the nearest door, which happened to be the library’s. At that moment she could think only of what he might say about her husband. She had not entered the room since the attack, and the servant had left the shutters closed. The narrow panes above them still admitted enough light to read.

“I hope you don’t mind the darkness,” Dorothea said, standing in the center of the room. “Since you banned books, we haven’t been using the library. But I hope Mr. Casaubon will soon return to it. Isn’t he improving?”
“Yes, far faster than I first anticipated. In fact, he’s already almost back to his usual health.”
“You aren’t afraid of another attack?” Her quick ear had caught a meaning beneath his tone.

“It’s particularly difficult to predict the course of a case like this,” Lydgate said. “The one thing I can say confidently is that we should take great care to prevent Mr. Casaubon from overtaxing his nervous strength in any way.”

“Please tell me plainly,” Dorothea begged. “I couldn’t bear to think there was something I hadn’t been told, something that would have changed my behavior if I’d known.” The words escaped like a cry, clearly expressing an experience still painfully close to her.
“Do sit down,” she added. She took the nearest chair and removed her bonnet and gloves, instinctively setting formality aside when so much was at stake.

“What you’ve just said confirms my own judgment,” Lydgate answered. “I believe a doctor should prevent regrets of that kind wherever possible. But please understand that your husband’s case is precisely the sort whose outcome is hardest to predict. He might live fifteen years or longer without being much less healthy than he has been until now.”
Dorothea had gone very pale. When he paused, she said quietly, “You mean if we take great care.”
“Yes. He needs protection against emotional disturbance of any kind, and against working too hard.”
“If he had to abandon his work, he’d be utterly unhappy,” she said, seeing that misery in a flash.

“I realize that. All we can do is use every direct and indirect means to make his occupations more varied and less demanding. If circumstances are favorable, as I said, there is no immediate danger from the heart condition I believe caused this attack. But it could develop more quickly. This is one of the conditions in which death can come suddenly. Nothing that might be affected by that possibility should be overlooked.”

For a few moments neither spoke. Dorothea sat as motionless as marble, though inwardly she was so intensely alive that never before had her mind passed over so many scenes and motives in so little time.
“Please help me,” she said at last, still in that low voice. “Tell me how I can help him.”
“Would a journey abroad be possible? You’ve recently been to Rome, haven’t you?”
The memories that made this suggestion utterly hopeless stirred a fresh current of feeling and broke her pale stillness.
“Oh, no, that wouldn’t help. Nothing could be worse,” she said with a more childlike despair, tears running down her face. “Nothing can do any good unless he enjoys it.”
“I wish I could have spared you this suffering,” Lydgate said. He was deeply moved, yet puzzled by her marriage. Women exactly like Dorothea had no place in his received ideas.
“You were right to tell me. I’m grateful you told me the truth.”

“I should make clear that I don’t intend to explain this to Mr. Casaubon himself. I think it best that he know only that he must avoid overwork and follow certain rules. Anxiety, whatever its cause, would be the very worst thing for him.”

Lydgate stood, and Dorothea rose automatically with him, undoing her cloak and throwing it aside as though she could not breathe in it. As he bowed to leave, an impulse that would have become a prayer had she been alone made her speak with a sob in her voice.

“Oh, surely you’re a wise man? You understand life and death. Tell me what to do. Think how I can help. He’s spent his whole life working and looking toward the future. He cares about nothing else. And nothing else matters to me—”

For years Lydgate remembered the effect of that unplanned appeal: one soul calling to another, aware only that their kindred natures moved through the same tangled world, the same troubled life lit by uncertain flashes. Yet what could he say now beyond promising to see Mr. Casaubon again the next day?

After he left, Dorothea burst into tears, releasing the pressure that had seemed to suffocate her. Then she dried her eyes, remembering that she must hide her distress from her husband. Looking around, she thought she must tell the servant to put the room in its usual order, since Mr. Casaubon might want to come in at any time now. Letters still lay untouched on his desk from the morning of his attack. Among them, as she remembered all too well, were Ladislaw’s, including her own unopened letter. Their painful associations had deepened with the sudden illness. She felt that the upset caused by her anger might have helped bring it on. She had not wanted to fetch the letters from the library: there would be time enough to read them when they were forced upon her again. Now, however, she thought they ought to be removed from her husband’s sight. Whatever had irritated him about them, he must be spared another irritation if possible. She first scanned the letter addressed to him, to find out whether a reply was needed to prevent the unwelcome visit.

Will was writing from Rome. He began by saying that he owed Mr. Casaubon so much that any thanks seemed presumptuous. Unless he were grateful, he would be the most contemptible scoundrel ever to find a generous friend. Elaborate expressions of gratitude would amount to announcing, “I’m honest.” But he had come to see that his faults, often pointed out by Mr. Casaubon himself, could be corrected only by a more demanding situation—the necessity his relative’s generosity had so far spared him. If any repayment were possible, he hoped to make the best one by proving the value of the education he owed to Mr. Casaubon and by no longer drawing on money to which others might have a better claim. He was returning to England to seek his fortune, as other young men with nothing but their brains had to do. His friend Naumann had asked him to take charge of the “Dispute,” the painting commissioned for Mr. Casaubon. With his and Mrs. Casaubon’s permission, Will would bring it to Lowick himself. If a visit would be inconvenient, a letter sent within the next fortnight to be held for him at the Paris post office would prevent it. He enclosed a letter to Mrs. Casaubon continuing a conversation about art they had begun in Rome.

Dorothea opened her letter and found a spirited continuation of his objections to her uncompromising sympathy for suffering, and to her lack of a robust, impartial delight in things as they were. It overflowed with youthful energy; just now she could not read it. The other letter required immediate action. There might still be time to keep Will from coming to Lowick. Eventually she gave it to her uncle, who was still in the house, and asked him to explain that Mr. Casaubon had been ill and was not well enough to receive visitors.

Nobody was more willing to write a letter than Mr. Brooke. His only difficulty was keeping it short. On this occasion his ideas spread over three large pages and into the inner folds. All he had said to Dorothea was:

“Of course I’ll write, my dear. A very clever young fellow, this Ladislaw. I expect he’ll make something of himself. A good letter, too—shows he understands things. Well, I’ll tell him about Casaubon.”

But the tip of Mr. Brooke’s pen was an organ of thought in its own right. It produced sentences, particularly kindly ones, before the rest of his mind could catch up. It voiced regrets and suggested solutions which, on rereading, struck him as wonderfully well phrased—surprisingly apt—and led him toward conclusions he had never previously considered. This time the pen thought it such a pity that young Ladislaw should miss coming to the neighborhood just now. Mr. Brooke could have got to know him better, and they could have examined the long-neglected Italian drawings together. The pen also took such an interest in a young man beginning life with a supply of ideas that, by the bottom of the second page, it had persuaded Mr. Brooke to invite Will to Tipton Grange instead of Lowick. Why not? There would be plenty for them to do together. This was a time of exceptional development; the political horizon was widening, and—in short, his pen launched into a little speech it had recently reported for the rather poorly edited “Middlemarch Pioneer.” As he sealed the letter, Mr. Brooke felt pleasantly stirred by a crowd of hazy plans. A young man who could put ideas into shape; the purchase of the “Pioneer” to prepare the way for a new candidate; documents put to use—who could say where it might all lead? Celia would soon be married, and having a young fellow at his table would be agreeable, at least for a while.
He left without telling Dorothea what he had written. She was occupied with her husband, and really these matters were of no concern to her.
